results.name: late_vs_early_discrimination
results.description: Correlation between each answer and its (set,target) cell's mean yes rate in the second half of each session (trial_index>=225) minus the same in the first half; positive vs the null means people get sharper/more consistent with the consensus as the session goes on (negative: noisier), which a static model cannot produce.

results.name: mersenne_fermat_target_contrast
results.description: In sets whose examples are all of the form 2^k-1 (e.g. 31,3,1,15) or all 2^k+1 (e.g. 33,17,5,9), yes rate for unshown odd targets of the same form minus yes rate for other odd targets; observed above the null means people use "one off a power of 2" concepts the model lacks (model under-produces the contrast).

results.name: majority_rule_exception_contrast
results.description: In sets of >=3 examples where all but exactly one example are multiples of some m in 3..12 (and not all are), yes rate for unshown multiples of m minus yes rate for unshown non-multiples; above the null means people keep the majority rule and discount the odd-one-out example more than the model (which only has power-of-2 exception rules and a uniform example-noise rate).
results.code:
# name: majority_rule_exception_contrast
# description: In sets of >=3 examples where all but exactly one example are multiples of some m in 3..12 (and not all are), yes rate for unshown multiples of m minus yes rate for unshown non-multiples; above the null means people keep the majority rule and discount the odd-one-out example more than the model (which only has power-of-2 exception rules and a uniform example-noise rate).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sv = sets.values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a_mask = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    b_mask = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        if len(ex) < 3:
            continue
        ms = [m for m in range(3, 13) if sum(e % m == 0 for e in ex) == len(ex) - 1]
        if not ms:
            continue
        m = max(ms)
        r = sv == s
        unshown = ~np.isin(t, ex)
        a_mask |= r & unshown & (t % m == 0)
        b_mask |= r & unshown & (t % m != 0)
    if a_mask.sum() == 0 or b_mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a_mask].mean() - y[b_mask].mean())

results.name: residual_lag1_autocorrelation
results.description: Within-participant correlation between consecutive answers' residuals (answer minus its (set,target) cell mean yes rate), participants split at trial_index==0; above the null means answers carry over from one trial to the next beyond what the stimuli explain (response perseveration/momentary bias the model lacks).
results.code:
# name: residual_lag1_autocorrelation
# description: Within-participant correlation between consecutive answers' residuals (answer minus its (set,target) cell mean yes rate), participants split at trial_index==0; above the null means answers carry over from one trial to the next beyond what the stimuli explain (response perseveration/momentary bias the model lacks).
def test_statistic(df):
    key = df["number_set"].astype(str) + "|" + df["target"].astype(str)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float)
    res = (y - y.groupby(key).transform("mean")).values
    pid = np.cumsum(df["trial_index"].astype(int).values == 0)
    same = pid[1:] == pid[:-1]
    a, b = res[1:][same], res[:-1][same]
    if a.std() == 0 or b.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1])

results.name: span_scaled_outside_generalization
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples with no shared parity, yes rate for targets just outside the span (distance <= 25% of span, at least 1) in wide sets (span>=40) minus the same in narrow sets (span<=15); above the null means generalization beyond the examples scales with their spread more than the model's interval-size principle predicts.
results.code:
# name: span_scaled_outside_generalization
# description: For sets of >=2 examples with no shared parity, yes rate for targets just outside the span (distance <= 25% of span, at least 1) in wide sets (span>=40) minus the same in narrow sets (span<=15); above the null means generalization beyond the examples scales with their spread more than the model's interval-size principle predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    arr = ex.apply(lambda v: [int(x) for x in v])
    lo = arr.map(min).values
    hi = arr.map(max).values
    n = arr.map(len).values
    npar = arr.map(lambda v: len({x % 2 for x in v})).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    span = hi - lo
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0))
    lim = np.maximum(1, 0.25 * span)
    base = (n >= 2) & (npar == 2) & (dist > 0) & (dist <= lim)
    w = base & (span >= 40)
    nr = base & (span <= 15)
    if w.sum() == 0 or nr.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[w].mean() - y[nr].mean())

results.name: participant_drift_sd
results.description: SD across participants (split at trial_index==0) of the change in yes rate from the first to the second half of their session; above the null means individuals drift in their yes-bias over time (some up, some down) more than a static model's sampling noise allows.
results.code:
# name: participant_drift_sd
# description: SD across participants (split at trial_index==0) of the change in yes rate from the first to the second half of their session; above the null means individuals drift in their yes-bias over time (some up, some down) more than a static model's sampling noise allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = np.cumsum(df["trial_index"].astype(int).values == 0)
    half = df["trial_index"].astype(int).values >= 225
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    d = pd.DataFrame({"p": pid, "h": half, "y": y})
    m = d.groupby(["p", "h"]).y.mean().unstack()
    m = m.dropna()
    if len(m) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float((m[True] - m[False]).std())

results.name: offset_progression_contrast
results.description: In two-example sets with gap d=|a-b| in 3..12 where the examples are not multiples of d, yes rate for unshown targets congruent to the examples mod d minus yes rate for other same-parity targets; observed above the null means people extend arithmetic progressions with an offset (e.g. 3,7 -> 11,15) that the model has no concept for.
results.code:
# name: offset_progression_contrast
# description: In two-example sets with gap d=|a-b| in 3..12 where the examples are not multiples of d, yes rate for unshown targets congruent to the examples mod d minus yes rate for other same-parity targets; observed above the null means people extend arithmetic progressions with an offset (e.g. 3,7 -> 11,15) that the model has no concept for.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    sv = sets.values
    a_mask = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    b_mask = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        if len(ex) != 2:
            continue
        d = abs(ex[0] - ex[1])
        if d < 3 or d > 12 or ex[0] % d == 0:
            continue
        r = sv == s
        cong = (t % d) == (ex[0] % d)
        same_par = (t % 2) == (ex[0] % 2)
        unshown = ~np.isin(t, ex)
        a_mask |= r & cong & unshown
        b_mask |= r & ~cong & same_par
    if a_mask.sum() == 0 or b_mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a_mask].mean() - y[b_mask].mean())

results.name: odd_rule_conjunction_contrast
results.description: In sets of >=2 all-odd examples that are all multiples of some m in {3,5,7,9} or all squares, yes rate for unshown odd members of that rule minus yes rate for even members of it; observed above the null means people infer the conjunction "odd AND rule" more sharply than the model's mixture of separate rules (model under-produces the contrast).
